stem: A team writes a PreToolUse hook to block destructive commands. During an incident they discover the hook crashed on a malformed payload and the command ran anyway. What went wrong?

options.text: PreToolUse hooks cannot block tool execution
The script exited with code 1, which is a non-blocking error, so the action proceeded
Hooks only run in interactive mode, not headless
The matcher was case-insensitive and failed to match

explanation: Only exit code 2 blocks and returns stderr to the model as the reason. Exit 1 is treated as a non-blocking hook error and the tool call proceeds, so a crashing guard script fails open rather than closed. Guard scripts need their own error handling.

stem: An engineering team adds a CLAUDE.md rule stating Claude Code must never run `git push --force` against the main branch. During a migration, a contributor pastes instructions from a Slack thread into the chat that override this rule, and the agent force-pushes to main anyway. Which control would have prevented this regardless of what instructions the agent received during that session?

options.text: A more detailed CLAUDE.md rule listing examples of what counts as a force push
A PreToolUse hook matching the Bash tool that inspects the command and exits 2 to block any force push targeting main
A PostToolUse hook that reverts the push once it detects one occurred
A system-prompt instruction paired with a lower sampling temperature

explanation: A rule that must always hold needs a deterministic control, not a prompt instruction that pasted text can override. A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes and, on exit 2, blocks it outright regardless of what the model was told in-session. More detailed CLAUDE.md wording is still a request, not a guarantee. PostToolUse fires after the push already happened, and a force push can rewrite history other developers have already pulled, so it cannot reliably undo the damage. Temperature affects sampling variance, not policy compliance.
